summary: For ages 9-10, teach children to read and complete real information tables — bus/train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and to solve one- and two-step problems: find a departure time, compute a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two difficulties carry the teaching: tracking a value to the correct ROW×COLUMN intersection (dense grids invite off-by-one reading), and computing time DURATIONS by counting on in minutes across the hour rather than subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals. Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.
misconceptions: Reading time as a decimal number: giving a journey duration as 0.70 or '2.23 hours' by subtracting or reading clock digits as base-10 rather than counting minutes in base-60
Reading off a single value when a difference or duration is asked ('how many more', 'how much longer') instead of computing it
Off-by-one-row/column reading: taking the value from an adjacent service or stop in a dense grid
In a two-way table, confusing a row/column TOTAL (a margin) with a single cell, or double-counting when categories overlap

activities.title: Live timetable with intersection highlighting
steps: Use a real bus/train timetable (often services in columns and stops in rows, but check the headings because layouts vary) to find when a named service reaches a named stop.

Track the stop-row with one finger and the service-column with the other, meeting at the intersecting cell. If a screen model is available, tapping a row and column can light up ONLY the intersecting cell so the off-by-one habit has nowhere to hide.

Find a journey duration by counting on in minutes across the hour: 10:50 → 11:00 is 10 minutes, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 minutes. If a duration tool is available, drag a marker along a minute-track and watch it tick across the hour.
State out loud why you cannot simply subtract 11:20 − 10:50 and call it 0.70 — the digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour.
activities.insight: Reading tables is a doing skill on a 2D grid: values live at a row×column intersection, and time durations are counted in minutes across the hour, not subtracted as decimals.

activities.title: Confront time-as-decimal with an analogue clock
steps: When a journey duration has been found by subtracting clock times as if they were decimals (e.g. 11:20 − 10:50 written as 0.70, or '70 minutes'), look at an analogue clock and state how many minutes are in one hour (60).
Find the correct duration in minutes by counting on from the start time to the end time across the hour on the clock face or an empty number line (e.g. 10:50 → 11:00 → 11:20 = 30 minutes).
Try a journey that crosses the hour in the other direction too — e.g. a train leaving at 14:45 with a 40-minute journey: when does it arrive?
Combine a lookup with a forward duration: if the next service is 25 minutes later than the one shown (say it leaves at 10:50), count on to find its departure time rather than adding digits.
activities.insight: The digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour, so durations must be counted in minutes, not read as decimals.

activities.title: Complete and interpret a two-way table
steps: Before any arithmetic, name what each cell, row total and column total MEANS (e.g. 'this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls').

Complete a missing cell in a two-way table of favourite sport by gender from the given data, checking the filled cell against its row and column totals. If a screen model is available, row and column totals can update live so a filled cell can be checked against its margins.
Answer a 'how many more' question — underline the question words, point to BOTH values, and show the subtraction.
Contrast with a plain 'how many' question so the difference between reading one value and computing a difference is explicit.
activities.insight: A cell, a row total and a column total mean different things; 'how many more' asks for a difference between two values, not a single read-off.

activities.title: Scorable checks on lookups, durations and cell completion
steps: Find a departure time from a shown timetable (selecting from options).
Complete 'the journey from A to B takes ___ minutes', including at least one item where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50→11:20).
Complete or fill a missing cell in a two-way table.
Answer one 'how many more' item that requires a difference, not a single value.
activities.insight: The reading-and-calculating procedure can be checked against items deliberately chosen to catch time-as-decimal and read-off-instead-of-difference errors.

activities.title: Annotated worked-example timetable (scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled timetable grid where the structure is annotated: services vs stops and what a single time cell means (and, on a two-way table, a single cell vs a row or column total), with tap-to-reveal explanations of what each part means.
Use it to rehearse naming the parts before doing your own lookups and durations on a live table.
activities.insight: Understanding the grid structure (services, stops and cells in a timetable; cells and totals in a two-way table) supports accurate reading before the child performs lookups and duration calculations independently.

checkQuestion: Put a real bus or train timetable (services in columns, several stops in rows) and a partly-completed two-way table (e.g. favourite sport by gender, with some cells and one total missing) in front of the child. Set these tasks and WATCH how they do them, saying little: (1) 'Find the time the 9:15 service reaches [named stop].' (2) 'How long does the journey from [stop A] to [stop B] take on that service?' — choose stops where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50 to 11:20). (3) 'Fill in the missing cell in this table, and tell me how many MORE girls than boys chose football.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not model the duration method or point to the right cell.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) the child tracks the correct row and column to their intersection and reads the right time; for (2) they compute the duration by counting on in minutes across the hour (10:50→11:20 = 30 minutes), not by subtracting the digits; for (3) they complete the cell using the right row and column (checking against a total if available) and give the DIFFERENCE between girls and boys, not a single value. Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the marks of mastery.
